description:
`local $SIG{ALRM} = sub { die "timeout\n" }; eval { alarm 5; system($slow) }`
is the everyday way to put a deadline on a child.  PCL's child-process
wrappers guarded themselves against a HOST error with a blanket
`(handler-case ... (error () -1))` -- #1920's rule that a child which cannot
be STARTED is a value, never a death -- and that guard also caught the
handler's die: the caller's eval saw an EMPTY $@ and the program carried on.

MEASURED perl -> base (5ce155cb) -> tree, six shapes
(scratch/s492c/logs/alarm-die-probes-s495.txt):

  case                      perl   BASE   TREE(before)  TREE(after)
  busy loop                 die    die    die           die
  sleep                     die    die    die           die
  system("sleep 4")         die    LOST   LOST          die
  `sleep 4` (backticks)     die    die    LOST  <-- s492c member 4's own
  waitpid($pid,0)           die    LOST   LOST          die
  wait()                    die    LOST   LOST          die

So the backtick half was this batch's REGRESSION and the other three were
pre-existing.  t/op/alarm.t row 3 ("alarm w/$SIG{ALRM} vs system()") IS the
system case: the snapshot says 5/0, the run measured 4/1, and a run of the
file on the BASE extraction measured 4/1 too.

FIX (f06bb8c9): ONE macro says what the guard means -- %p-child-host-error
runs its body, answers the failure value on a HOST error and RE-SIGNALS a perl
death, decided by the one existing predicate %p-perl-die-p.  p-system, p-wait
and p-waitpid use it; p-backtick keeps only the run-program call inside it, so
the read and the wait sit outside any guard.  #1920's own path is unchanged
and is in the guard row: system("no-such-prog","a") is still -1 with $! set.
op/alarm.t is back to 5/0 without any baseline edit.

Normative statement: docs/ir-spec.md 7.5b (the paragraph after the table).
Guard: one row in Pl/t/system-block-01.t (36 -> 37), inverse-verified on a
